title.en: Best-of-N: Let a Verifier Pick the Winner

description.en: Voting works when many samples agree — but sometimes the right answer is rare and unusual, not popular. Best-of-N sampling fixes that: generate N candidates, score each with a verifier, and keep the highest-scoring one.

story_variants.en:
## When The Crowd Isn't Right, Grade Instead Of Counting

"Majority voting assumes the correct answer is the *popular* one," Vaathiyaar says. "But for a hard coding problem, the correct fix might come from exactly one clever sample out of ten, while nine ordinary samples all share the same *wrong* answer. Counting votes would pick the wrong one."

### Best-of-N Sampling

**Best-of-N** takes a different approach to the same test-time-compute budget: generate N candidate completions, run each one through a **verifier** — a reward model, a unit test, a scoring function — and keep whichever candidate scores highest. No counting, no popularity contest: one number per candidate, take the max.

```
candidate 1 -> reward 0.62
candidate 2 -> reward 0.91   <- best
candidate 3 -> reward 0.77

best_of_n -> candidate 2
```

This is the same mechanism behind RLHF-style reward models picking the best response, and behind code-generation pipelines that run N candidate solutions against unit tests and ship whichever one passes with the highest score.

### Best-of-N vs. Self-Consistency

Both spend the same kind of budget — N samples of the same prompt — but they pick a winner differently:

- **Self-consistency** needs answers that are easy to *compare for equality* (so they can be counted), and wins when the right answer is the *popular* one.
- **Best-of-N** needs a *scoring function*, and wins when the right answer is *identifiable* even if it's rare — as long as the verifier can tell good from bad.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** if you can count matching answers, vote. If you can score quality, take the best. Both are test-time compute; the difference is what you do with the N samples once you have them.

Today you implement the Best-of-N selection step, plus a metric for how much it gained over an average single sample.
